title: Refining the Architecture of the Quadruple Pre-main-sequence System HD 98800: Improved Orbits, Dynamical Masses, and a Transiting Circumbinary Disk
comment: 21 pages including figures and tables. Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: We present new spectroscopic and interferometric observations of the pre-main-sequence hierarchical quadruple system HD 98800, a member of the nearby TW Hya association. Our radial velocity monitoring extends the total coverage to over 36 years, sampling the periastron passage in the $\sim$240-yr outer orbit. By combining these velocities with new and archival interferometric observations of both inner binaries (A and B), we significantly refine the system orbits and constrain the dynamical masses of all four stars to $\leq$ 2.6 percent. The resulting stellar properties (masses, effective temperatures, and absolute magnitudes) are found to agree well with current stellar evolution models. Notably, binary B hosts a known circumbinary disk in a polar orientation. Our interferometric imaging, as well as ground-based photometry by others, capture binary A currently passing directly behind the disk, a striking alignment given the outer orbit's long period. We use the photometry to infer the optical extinction produced by the disk material. The eclipse is expected to last about a decade, and offers an unprecedented opportunity to probe the structure and composition of the potentially planet-forming disk. Our refined orbits and component masses provide a robust dynamical framework to support ongoing and future studies of this unique event.

AI.tldr: New spectroscopy and interferometry of the hierarchical quadruple system HD 98800 refine all four stellar orbits and yield dynamical masses accurate to ≤2.6%, revealing that binary A is currently eclipsed by binary B's polar circumbinary disk—a decade-long event offering a rare probe of disk structure.
AI.motivation: HD 98800 is a nearby young hierarchical quadruple system whose outer orbit (~240 yr) and four component masses were poorly constrained, limiting dynamical benchmarking of stellar evolution models and interpretation of its unusual circumbinary disk geometry.
AI.method: Combined 36+ yr of radial velocity monitoring (sampling periastron of the outer orbit) with new and archival interferometric observations of inner binaries A and B to fit improved orbital solutions, derive dynamical masses, and compare stellar properties with evolutionary models; interferometric imaging and ground-based photometry characterize the ongoing eclipse of binary A by binary B's polar circumbinary disk, from which optical extinction is inferred.
AI.result: All four stellar masses are constrained to ≤2.6% precision; masses, effective temperatures, and absolute magnitudes agree with current stellar evolution models. Interferometry and photometry capture binary A passing directly behind the polar circumbinary disk of binary B, with estimated optical extinction and an expected eclipse duration of about a decade.
AI.conclusion: The refined orbits and component masses provide a robust dynamical framework and a unique, time-limited opportunity to probe the structure and composition of a potentially planet-forming circumbinary disk through the decade-long eclipse, supporting ongoing and future studies.

title: A Meta-analysis of Chemical Abundances Derived from Ultraviolet and Optical Lines of Os, Ir, and Pt, and a Reassessment of the Robustness of the Third r-process Peak in Metal-poor Stars
comment: Accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal (19 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables)
summary: We reassess the abundance ratio between elements at the third rapid neutron-capture process (r-process) peak (Os, Ir, Pt) and the lanthanide element Eu. We show that some weak optical lines of Os I, Ir I, and Pt I yield abundances inconsistent with stronger ultraviolet (UV) and optical lines and provide recommendations for their limited use alongside more reliable lines. We perform a meta-analysis of Os, Ir, and Pt abundances from 35 studies of 77 r-process-enhanced metal-poor stars spanning -3.43 < [Fe/H] < -1.27 and +0.22 < [Eu/Fe] < +2.45. The mean third-peak to lanthanide abundance ratios are $\log\varepsilon$(Os/Eu) = 0.86 $\pm$ 0.02, $\log\varepsilon$(Ir/Eu) = 0.88 $\pm$ 0.03, and $\log\varepsilon$(Pt/Eu) = 1.12 $\pm$ 0.04, which agree with the inferred Solar System r-process ratios to within 0.05 dex. These abundance ratios vary by less than 0.50 dex (a factor of 3.2), 0.56 dex (a factor of 3.6), and 0.45 dex (a factor of 2.8), respectively, in 90 percent of the r-process events that enriched metal-poor stars in existing samples. We use a representative r-process model to show that the small range of stellar abundance ratios favor models with a substantial contribution from neutron-rich material, with electron fractions, $Y_e$, < 0.2. We conclude that the third-peak to lanthanide abundance ratios are robust in existing r-process-enhanced star samples. In two stars with [Eu/Fe] < 0, the upper limits derived from non-detection of Pt indicate that the third-peak elements are deficient relative to lanthanides, and we conclude that this may be a signature of the limited r-process.

AI.tldr: A meta-analysis of 35 studies of 77 r-process-enhanced metal-poor stars shows that third-peak (Os, Ir, Pt) to Eu abundance ratios are consistent with Solar System r-process ratios and vary by less than ~0.5 dex, favoring neutron-rich r-process models with Y_e < 0.2.
AI.motivation: The third r-process peak to lanthanide ratio is a key diagnostic of r-process conditions, but earlier abundance determinations—especially from weak optical lines—are potentially unreliable, and no systematic reassessment of the ratio across the full sample of r-process-enhanced metal-poor stars had been made.
AI.method: The authors flag spurious weak optical Os I, Ir I, and Pt I lines whose abundances disagree with stronger UV/optical lines and recommend restricted use. They then perform a meta-analysis of Os, Ir, and Pt abundances compiled from 35 studies of 77 r-process-enhanced metal-poor stars (-3.43 < [Fe/H] < -1.27, +0.22 < [Eu/Fe] < +2.45), and compare the resulting third-peak/Eu ratios with Solar System r-process values and with predictions of a representative r-process model.
AI.result: Mean ratios are log ε(Os/Eu) = 0.86 ± 0.02, log ε(Ir/Eu) = 0.88 ± 0.03, and log ε(Pt/Eu) = 1.12 ± 0.04, agreeing with inferred Solar System r-process ratios within 0.05 dex. The ratios scatter by less than 0.50, 0.56, and 0.45 dex (factors of 3.2, 3.6, 2.8) in 90% of the r-process events sampled. The narrow spread favors models with substantial neutron-rich material (Y_e < 0.2). In two stars with [Eu/Fe] < 0, Pt non-detection upper limits indicate third-peak elements are deficient relative to lanthanides.
AI.conclusion: Third-peak to lanthanide abundance ratios are robust in existing r-process-enhanced star samples and match the Solar System r-process pattern. The small observed scatter supports neutron-rich (Y_e < 0.2) r-process conditions. Deficiency of third-peak elements relative to lanthanides in [Eu/Fe] < 0 stars may signal a limited r-process.

title: Multi-vantage SO/PHI and SDO/HMI magnetic field observations of active region NOAA 13465
summary:
Context. Until the launch of Solar Orbiter, long term studies of active region magnetic fields were restricted to a single vantage point: that from Earth. What further restricted these studies were geometrical effects, such as foreshortening and projection, that plague magnetic field observations when the active region was away from the central meridian.
  Aims. To track an active region, in this case NOAA 13465, with Solar Orbiter during a perihelion pass and use co-observations made by SDO/HMI and SO/PHI-HRT from different vantage points to explore the systematics plaguing observations away from disc centre.
  Methods. We use the SHARP (Space-Weather HMI Active Region Patches) data series from SDO/HMI, and create similar datasets with SO/PHI-HRT observations. We compare and contrast the line-of-sight and the three heliographic magnetic field components. Finally we compare the unsigned radial flux, and unsigned totals of the northward and westward magnetic components using the SHARP masking method to select a common area.
  Results. We find that the instrument observing closer to the limb infers a greater unsigned radial magnetic flux compared to that observing at disc centre, with a maximum near approximately $45^\circ$. The plage displayed more susceptibility to resolution and projection effects than the active region's sole sunspot. In particular the deduced area of the solar plage drove the observed increase in flux near the limb. Thanks to its higher spatial resolution, the SO/PHI-HRT data showed a smaller effect compared to SDO/HMI near the limb, highlighting a dependence on instrument resolution. Finally, the ratio of the two instruments' vertical magnetic flux exhibits a strong positive correlation with the ratio of the cosine of the instruments' viewing angles.

AI.tldr: Tracking NOAA 13465 with Solar Orbiter and SDO/HMI from different vantage points reveals that the instrument viewing closer to the limb infers larger unsigned radial flux (max near ~45°), with plage more susceptible to projection/resolution effects than the sunspot; higher-resolution SO/PHI-HRT shows reduced limb bias, confirming a resolution dependence.
AI.motivation: Long-term active region magnetic field studies were historically limited to a single vantage point (Earth), and were further compromised by geometrical effects such as foreshortening and projection that degrade magnetic observations away from the central meridian. Solar Orbiter enables multi-vantage-point co-observations to characterize these systematics.
AI.method: The authors applied the SHARP (Space-Weather HMI Active Region Patches) data series from SDO/HMI and constructed analogous datasets from SO/PHI-HRT observations of NOAA 13465 during a perihelion pass. They compared line-of-sight and three heliographic magnetic field components, and compared unsigned radial flux and unsigned totals of the northward and westward components within a common area selected via the SHARP masking method.
AI.result: The instrument viewing closer to the limb inferred a greater unsigned radial magnetic flux than that observing at disc centre, peaking near ~45°. Plage showed greater susceptibility to resolution and projection effects than the sunspot, and the deduced plage area drove the flux increase near the limb. SO/PHI-HRT exhibited a smaller effect than SDO/HMI near the limb owing to higher spatial resolution. The ratio of the two instruments' vertical magnetic flux correlated strongly and positively with the ratio of the cosines of their viewing angles.
AI.conclusion: Projection and resolution effects bias radial flux estimates away from disc centre, with plage area being the dominant driver; higher instrument resolution mitigates this bias. The vertical flux ratio scales with the cosine view-angle ratio, offering a systematic characterization of vantage-point-dependent observation errors.

title: The Eclipsing $γ$ Doradus Star VZ Canum Venaticorum
comment: 9 pages, including 4 figures and 3 tables, accepted for publication in PASJ
summary: We present a detailed analysis of the eclipsing binary VZ CVn using TESS Sectors 50 and 77 photometry together with published spectroscopic results. The TESS light curves were modeled to refine the binary parameters, and the residual light curves were analyzed to investigate the pulsational properties of the system. We derive masses and radii of $M_{\rm A}=1.526\pm0.005$ $M_\odot$ and $R_{\rm A}=1.638\pm0.023$ $R_\odot$ for the primary and $M_{\rm B}=1.259\pm0.005$ $M_\odot$ and $R_{\rm B}=1.133\pm0.016$ $R_\odot$ for the secondary. Comparison with PARSEC evolutionary models suggests a near-solar metallicity of $Z=0.017$ and an age of 1.0 Gyr. Separate frequency analyses of the two TESS sectors reveal four signals with possible counterparts in both sectors. Two of these frequencies, $f_2=4.7486$ day$^{-1}$ and $f_6=7.1242$ day$^{-1}$, are consistent with the fourth and sixth orbital harmonics, respectively, suggesting an orbital origin rather than independent $δ$ Sct pulsations. The dominant frequency $f_1=1.7577$ day$^{-1}$ has a pulsation constant of $Q_1=0.336$ day, consistent with a $γ$ Dor-type g-mode pulsation. The weaker signal $f_5=1.9754$ day$^{-1}$ also has a pulsation constant of $Q_5=0.299$ day, although its detection remains tentative because of its low S/N. Together with the physical and evolutionary properties of the primary, these results support its classification as a $γ$ Dor pulsator rather than the previously proposed $γ$ Dor--$δ$ Sct hybrid pulsator.

AI.tldr: TESS-based reanalysis of eclipsing binary VZ CVn yields refined masses/radii, near-solar metallicity at ~1 Gyr, and evidence that the primary is a γ Dor pulsator rather than a γ Dor–δ Sct hybrid.
AI.motivation: To refine the physical and orbital parameters of VZ CVn and to clarify the pulsational nature of its components, in particular to test the earlier claim that the primary is a γ Dor–δ Sct hybrid pulsator.
AI.method: Modeling of TESS Sectors 50 and 77 light curves to refine binary parameters; residual-light-curve analysis and separate frequency analyses of both sectors; comparison with PARSEC evolutionary models; pulsation-constant (Q) diagnostics and checks against orbital harmonics.
AI.result: Primary: M_A = 1.526 ± 0.005 M_sun, R_A = 1.638 ± 0.023 R_sun; secondary: M_B = 1.259 ± 0.005 M_sun, R_B = 1.133 ± 0.016 R_sun. PARSEC fitting gives Z = 0.017 and age ≈ 1.0 Gyr. Four frequencies recur across sectors; f2 = 4.7486 d^-1 and f6 = 7.1242 d^-1 match the fourth and sixth orbital harmonics (orbital origin). Dominant f1 = 1.7577 d^-1 has Q1 = 0.336 d (γ Dor g-mode); f5 = 1.9754 d^-1 has Q5 = 0.299 d but is tentative (low S/N).
AI.conclusion: The physical and evolutionary properties plus the pulsation-constant diagnostics support classifying the primary of VZ CVn as a γ Dor pulsator, superseding the previously proposed γ Dor–δ Sct hybrid classification.

title: A Wideband Technosignature Search of 210,191 Nearby Main-sequence Stars with the VLA Sky Survey
comment: 30 pages, 9 figures. Submitted to AAS Journals
summary: Searches for radio technosignatures have concentrated on narrowband signals. We present a complementary search for excess broadband 2-4 GHz emission from 210,191 Gaia DR3 main-sequence stars within 100 pc in all epochs of the VLA Sky Survey (VLASS; 2017-2026). Cross-matching with the Epoch-1 catalog yields 51 high-reliability positional associations (versus 1.5 expected by chance). All but one are known natural emitters that, where measurable, move with their stars; the remaining source, near LSPM J1943+5337, is not at the star. Because stellar flares can mimic transmitters in continuum flux, a detection counts as a possible transmitter at any luminosity only at the 32,985 apparently single AFGK stars outside known radio-emitter classes, and at M dwarfs and AFGK multiples only above $10^{10}$ W Hz$^{-1}$. Forced photometry of 208,232 stars in all epochs finds 1 steady-test detection and 3 stars detected in at least one epoch among the eligible stars, against 1.3 and 1.9 expected by chance. The median per-star limit on steady emission is $L_ν<4.0\times10^{8}$ W Hz$^{-1}$. Without background subtraction, fewer than $1.5\times10^{-4}$ of eligible AFGK stars host a steady transmitter above $10^9$ W Hz$^{-1}$, and fewer than $2.3\times10^{-5}$ of all stars outside the known-emitter classes host one above $\sim1.1\times10^{10}$ W Hz$^{-1}$; counting every M-dwarf detection as a possible transmitter, fewer than $5.5\times10^{-4}$ of M dwarfs host one above $10^9$ W Hz$^{-1}$. Stacks detect population-averaged emission from M dwarfs, concentrated in those with activity evidence. Continuum surveys thus constrain broadband, modulated, or rapidly drifting signals that narrowband pipelines do not search for.

AI.tldr: A complementary broadband (2–4 GHz) technosignature search of 210,191 nearby Gaia DR3 main-sequence stars in VLASS epochs finds no significant excess emission attributable to extraterrestrial transmitters, placing tight upper limits on the prevalence of steady broadband emitters (e.g., <1.5×10⁻⁴ of eligible AFGK stars above 10⁹ W Hz⁻¹).
AI.motivation: Prior radio technosignature searches have focused almost exclusively on narrowband signals, leaving broadband, modulated, or rapidly drifting emission poorly constrained. Stellar flares are also known to mimic transmitters in continuum flux, so a careful search must distinguish natural stellar emission from possible artificial sources.
AI.method: Cross-matched 210,191 Gaia DR3 main-sequence stars within 100 pc against all VLASS epochs (2017–2026), yielding 51 high-reliability positional associations (vs. 1.5 expected by chance). Treated stellar flares as contaminants by defining detection criteria: possible transmitters at any luminosity only for 32,985 apparently single AFGK stars outside known radio-emitter classes, and above 10¹⁰ W Hz⁻¹ for M dwarfs and AFGK multiples. Performed forced photometry on 208,232 stars across all epochs, applied background subtraction analysis, and used stacking to probe population-averaged emission.
AI.result: Of 51 positional associations, all but one are known natural emitters that (where measurable) move with their stars; the remaining source near LSPM J1943+5337 is not at the star. Forced photometry found 1 steady-test detection and 3 stars detected in ≥1 epoch among eligible stars, vs. 1.3 and 1.9 expected by chance. Median per-star limit on steady emission is L_ν < 4.0×10⁸ W Hz⁻¹. Without background subtraction, <1.5×10⁻⁴ of eligible AFGK stars host a steady transmitter above 10⁹ W Hz⁻¹, <2.3×10⁻⁵ of all stars outside known-emitter classes host one above ~1.1×10¹⁰ W Hz⁻¹, and (counting every M-dwarf detection as a possible transmitter) <5.5×10⁻⁴ of M dwarfs host one above 10⁹ W Hz⁻¹. Stacks detect population-averaged emission from M dwarfs, concentrated in those with activity evidence.
AI.conclusion: No compelling broadband technosignature candidates were identified; the results yield stringent upper limits on the fraction of nearby stars hosting steady broadband transmitters. The study demonstrates that continuum surveys provide complementary constraints on broadband, modulated, or rapidly drifting signals that narrowband pipelines cannot detect, while confirming that stellar activity drives the detectable radio emission in the sample.

title: Quiet-Sun magnetic field configuration inferred from the ratio of longitudinal fields measured in the Fe I λ6301 and λ6302 Å lines
summary: The estimate of the longitudinal magnetic field obtained from the Hinode spectropolarimeter data will be different if it is determined in different ways. In particular, the values obtained by the Center Of Gravity (COG) method for the Fe I $λ$ 6301 and 6302 $Å$ lines do not coincide. Some of the differences are due to the different inaccuracies of the COG method for each of the two lines. However, some of the differences can be explained by the fact that the response functions of these lines to changes in the magnetic field are formed at different heights. This should be accompanied by a certain morphological structure of magnetic fields. It consists in the fact that most of the magnetic configurations of the quiet photosphere are similar to each other. To a rough approximation, their structure can be compared with the structure of a sunspot - there is a central region with the strongest field, close to vertical, and slopes - an analog of penumbra, where the field weakens and / or turns to horizontal. This turn occurs at the heights of the greatest response of the Fe I $λ$ 6301 and 6302 $Å$ lines to changes in the magnetic field with a turn length of about tens of kilometers.

AI.tldr: Discrepancies between Center-of-Gravity magnetic field estimates from the Fe I 6301 and 6302 Å lines arise partly from line-specific COG inaccuracies and partly because each line's magnetic response forms at different heights, implying a shallow sunspot-like magnetic morphology in the quiet photosphere.
AI.motivation: Hinode spectropolarimeter longitudinal field estimates depend on the retrieval method: the COG values from Fe I 6301 and 6302 Å do not agree, and this inconsistency needs physical explanation rather than being dismissed as methodological noise.
AI.method: Comparative analysis of COG-derived longitudinal field estimates for the two Fe I lines, decomposing differences into intrinsic COG inaccuracies versus height-dependent response functions, interpreted through a morphological model of magnetic configuration.
AI.result: Part of the 6301/6302 discrepancy is attributable to differing COG errors per line; the remainder reflects response functions formed at different heights. Quiet-photosphere magnetic configurations are argued to resemble a sunspot: a central near-vertical strong-field core plus sloping penumbra-like flanks where the field weakens and/or turns horizontal, with the turn occurring at the peak-response heights and spanning tens of kilometers.
AI.conclusion: Line-pair disagreement is a diagnostic of height stratification: the field turn is located near the response heights of the 6301/6302 Å lines over a horizontal scale of order tens of km, implying a common, compact, sunspot-like field geometry in the quiet photosphere.

title: Nonlinear models of Mira variables with long secondary periods
comment: 11 pages, 6 figures, accepted to Astronomy Letters
summary: Calculations of nonlinear radial oscillations in asymptotic giant branch stars with an initial mass of $M_\mathrm{ZAMS}=1.6M_\odot$ were performed for initial helium and metal abundances of $Y=0.28$ and $Z=0.006$, respectively. Several models from the evolutionary sequence after the 4th thermal pulse were used as initial conditions for the hydrodynamic equations describing stellar pulsations with long secondary periods. Using the discrete Fourier transform of the hydrodynamic solutions we show that long secondary periods appear in Mira variables pulsating simultaneously in the fundamental mode and first overtone with non-multiple periods. The relative deviation from multiplicity is $δ_\mathrmΠ\le 1.2\times 10^{-2}$ and is responsible for mode splitting into equally spaced frequency components, each of which is a standing wave with a free outer boundary. The cycle length of long secondary periods is nearly 20 times that of the fundamental mode. Long secondary periodicity is a nonlinear effect that arises after reaching the limiting amplitude and develops over several hundred fundamental mode periods.

AI.tldr: Nonlinear radial oscillations of an AGB star (1.6 M⊙) show that long secondary periods (LSPs) arise from simultaneous fundamental-mode and first-overtone pulsation with slightly non-multiple periods, generating split, equally spaced frequency components.
AI.motivation: The origin of long secondary periods (LSPs) observed in Mira variables and AGB stars remains unexplained; the authors test whether LSPs can emerge naturally from nonlinear pulsation dynamics rather than requiring binary or other external mechanisms.
AI.method: Hydrodynamic simulations of nonlinear radial oscillations using stellar models from the evolutionary sequence after the 4th thermal pulse (M_ZAMS = 1.6 M⊙, Y = 0.28, Z = 0.006) as initial conditions; discrete Fourier transform analysis of the hydrodynamic solutions.
AI.result: LSPs appear when the star pulsates simultaneously in the fundamental mode and first overtone with non-multiple periods; the relative deviation from multiplicity is δ_Π ≤ 1.2×10⁻², causing mode splitting into equally spaced frequency components, each a standing wave with a free outer boundary. The LSP cycle length is nearly 20 times the fundamental-mode period.
AI.conclusion: LSP is a nonlinear effect that emerges after the pulsation reaches its limiting amplitude and develops over several hundred fundamental-mode periods, providing a self-consistent, purely pulsational explanation for long secondary periods in Mira variables.

title: Robustness of Transition Probabilities of Spectral Lines Deduced from Spatially Resolved Solar Spectra
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A; abstract abridged for arxiv; 15 pages
summary: Atomic parameters are a key ingredient for the synthesis of spectral lines to model observed spectra and to extract meaningful physical information about the observed astrophysical object. We use quiet-sun observations to test the reliability of the atomic parameter inference from observed spectra. Our focus is on the transition probability of spectral lines, denoted as log(gf). We apply a spectropolarimetric inversion method to quiet-sun disc-centre observations at 1.56 $μ$m from the GRIS/GREGOR spectrograph. We use the coupled method implemented in the globin inversion code, where atomic parameters are spatially coupled, and a single value of these parameters is determined for every spectral line over the entire field of view. We carry out tests to determine the sensitivity of the inferred log(gf) values to various atmospheric parameters and the data reduction fallibility. We find that our log(gf) values are weaker by 0.023 dex compared to the most recent study. This is most probably caused by the constraint imposed on the log(gf) parameter due to the spatial coupling, lifting the degeneracy between temperature and log(gf). We use the Markov chain Monte Carlo method to determine the uncertainty in the inferred log(gf) values. For the strongest lines in the spectral region, the uncertainty in log(gf) is 1-4 %, increasing to 12 % for weaker and blended lines. Our tests suggest that the log(gf) values inferred using the coupled method from globin are robust against any local contamination to the observed line profiles, such as spectral stray light, and return a reliable and unique set of log(gf) values for the strongest lines irrespective of the chosen atmospheric model and observation dataset. This result is valid as long as the underlying assumptions of line formation under local thermodynamic equilibrium and the completeness of the line list are satisfied.

AI.tldr: Quiet-sun spectropolarimetric observations at 1.56 μm are inverted with the coupled globin method to infer transition probabilities (log(gf)); the results show robust, uniquely determined log(gf) values for strong lines, with 1–4% uncertainties, but about 0.023 dex weaker than previous values.
AI.motivation: Atomic parameters such as log(gf) are essential for synthesizing spectral lines, modeling observed spectra, and extracting physical information about astrophysical objects. The authors aim to test how reliably these parameters can be inferred directly from observed spectra.
AI.method: A spectropolarimetric inversion is applied to quiet-sun disc-centre observations at 1.56 μm from the GRIS/GREGOR spectrograph, using the coupled method in the globin inversion code, where atomic parameters are spatially coupled and a single log(gf) value is determined per spectral line over the whole field of view. Sensitivity tests are performed for various atmospheric parameters and data-reduction fallibility, and MCMC is used to estimate uncertainties.
AI.result: Inferred log(gf) values are about 0.023 dex weaker than the most recent study, likely due to the spatial coupling lifting the temperature–log(gf) degeneracy. Uncertainties are 1–4% for the strongest lines and up to 12% for weaker, blended lines. The values are robust against local contamination such as spectral stray light and yield a reliable, unique set for strong lines regardless of atmospheric model or dataset.
AI.conclusion: The coupled globin method provides robust and unique log(gf) estimates for strong lines, valid provided the assumptions of LTE line formation and line-list completeness hold.

title: The evolution of discs and the epoch of formation of giant planets around low-mass stars
comment: 12 pages, 13 figures, 4 appendices with tables and figures
summary: Large-grain depletion in the inner discs of young stellar systems provides a potential observational signature of dust filtration by forming giant-planet cores. In a previous study, we found that $0.50\pm0.10$ of prominent protoplanetary discs around solar-type stars ($0.7$--$1.5$~\Msun) with ages of 2--8~Myr show evidence for a depletion of large grains inside the snow line. Such a depletion may arise when a sufficiently massive planetary core acts as a barrier to the inward drift of large grains, filtering them from the inner disc. If this interpretation is correct, the frequency of dust-filtration signatures should decrease towards lower stellar masses, in accordance with the lower occurrence rate of giant planets around low-mass stars. Extending our analysis to lower-mass stars, we found that only $0.09\pm0.09$ of discs around stars with masses of $0.30$--$0.58$~\Msun, corresponding to the progenitors of main-sequence early M-type stars, show evidence of grain filtration. This fraction is lower than that measured for solar-type stars and is consistent with the lower frequency of giant planets around M-type stars. We also found that discs exhibiting evidence of filtration tend to have relatively massive outer dust reservoirs, with dust masses exceeding $20$~\MEarth. Conversely, the absence of filtration signatures in lower-mass discs suggests that Neptune-mass and lower-mass planets, despite being common around low-mass stars, may generally be unable to filter large grains efficiently.

AI.tldr: Large-grain depletion inside the snow line (a sign of dust filtration by forming giant-planet cores) is found in only 0.09±0.09 of discs around 0.30–0.58 Msun stars, versus 0.50±0.10 for solar-type stars, consistent with the lower occurrence of giant planets around lower-mass stars. Filtration is associated with massive outer dust reservoirs (>20 MEarth), and low-mass (Neptune-class) planets appear unable to filter large grains efficiently.
AI.motivation: Large-grain depletion in inner discs may be an observational signature of dust filtration by growing giant-planet cores. If correct, the frequency of such signatures should scale with stellar mass, mirroring the lower giant-planet occurrence around low-mass stars, so extending the analysis to lower-mass stars provides a test of the filtration interpretation.
AI.method: Extend a prior analysis of prominent protoplanetary discs to stars of 0.30–0.58 Msun (progenitors of early M-type main-sequence stars), quantifying the fraction of discs showing evidence of large-grain depletion inside the snow line and comparing with the 0.50±0.10 fraction found for solar-type stars (0.7–1.5 Msun, ages 2–8 Myr); also relate filtration signatures to outer dust reservoir masses.
AI.result: Only 0.09±0.09 of discs around 0.30–0.58 Msun stars show evidence of grain filtration, significantly lower than the solar-type value and consistent with the lower giant-planet frequency around M-type stars. Discs showing filtration tend to have massive outer dust reservoirs exceeding 20 MEarth.
AI.conclusion: The stellar-mass dependence of dust-filtration signatures supports the interpretation that they trace giant-planet cores. The absence of filtration signatures in lower-mass discs implies that Neptune-mass and lower-mass planets, though common around low-mass stars, are generally unable to filter large grains efficiently.

title: Photometric Characterisation and Evolutionary State Investigation of the Low Mass-Ratio Contact Binary FASTT 1558
comment: 24 pages, 13 figures, 9 tables, accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Contact binaries with low mass ratios, as potential progenitors of stellar mergers, offer important insights into the physical processes governing mass and energy transfer. In this work, we present the first spectro-photometry based evolutionary investigation of FASTT 1558, a totally eclipsing, low mass-ratio contact binary. We combine TESS and ASAS-SN photometry with phase-resolved spectroscopy obtained with the 3.6m Devasthal Optical Telescope. The lightcurve modeling with PHOEBE shows that the system has an exceptionally low secondary-to-primary mass ratio of $q=0.1544\pm0.0013$, with a deep contact degree of $f=0.61\pm0.01$. Our analysis yields a total system mass of $1.92\pm0.31\,M_\odot$, while the distance to the system is estimated to be $648.45\pm29.85$ pc. Analysis of long-term eclipse timings reveals an apparent orbital period decrease of $\dot{P}=-(3.03\pm0.26) \times 10^{-7}$ ${\rm day\,yr^{-1}}$, which may be associated with mass-transfer from the primary to the secondary on a thermal timescale. The spectra show phase-dependent H$α$ and CaII equivalent widths, indicating a dynamically evolving chromosphere. Binary evolution calculations with MESA terminates through L2 overflow before reaching the observed low mass-ratio. Despite its extreme mass ratio, the system is presently Darwin stable, with $J_{\rm spin}/J_{\rm orb}=0.15\pm0.02$. FASTT 1558 therefore provides a robust observational benchmark for evolutionary models of low mass-ratio contact binaries.

AI.tldr: FASTT 1558 is a totally eclipsing, low-mass-ratio contact binary (q=0.1544, f=0.61) characterized via joint TESS/ASAS-SN photometry and phase-resolved spectroscopy, revealing an orbital period decrease consistent with thermal-timescale mass transfer, phase-dependent chromospheric activity, and present-day Darwin stability (J_spin/J_orb=0.15) despite its extreme mass ratio.
AI.motivation: Low-mass-ratio contact binaries are potential progenitors of stellar mergers, so they provide key constraints on the physical processes of mass and energy transfer. The authors aim to provide a robust observational benchmark for evolutionary models of such extreme systems.
AI.method: The authors combine TESS and ASAS-SN photometry with phase-resolved spectroscopy from the 3.6 m Devasthal Optical Telescope. Light-curve modeling is performed with PHOEBE; long-term eclipse timing (O-C) analysis is used to measure the period change; spectra are used to measure phase-dependent Hα and CaII equivalent widths; and MESA binary evolution calculations are carried out for comparison.
AI.result: The system has q=0.1544±0.0013 and contact degree f=0.61±0.01, with total mass 1.92±0.31 M_sun and distance 648.45±29.85 pc. Eclipse timings show an orbital period decrease of dP/dt=-(3.03±0.26)×10^-7 day/yr, possibly linked to thermal-timescale mass transfer from the primary to the secondary. Spectra show phase-dependent Hα and CaII equivalent widths, indicating a dynamically evolving chromosphere. MESA evolution terminates through L2 overflow before reaching the observed mass ratio. The system is currently Darwin stable with J_spin/J_orb=0.15±0.02.
AI.conclusion: FASTT 1558, despite its extreme mass ratio, is presently Darwin stable and shows evidence of ongoing mass transfer and chromospheric activity. It serves as a robust observational benchmark for evolutionary models of low-mass-ratio contact binaries.

title: A catalog of Gaia DR3 luminous blue variables and candidate luminous blue variables
summary: Galactic LBVs are rare, evolved massive stars whose defining evidence is long-term spectroscopic and photometric instability, including S Doradus-type cycles, and, in exceptional cases, giant eruptions. Candidate LBVs (cLBVs) share LBV-like spectra and/or circumstellar nebulae; however, they lack long-term observational datasets that would detect their long-term variability and confirm their classification as bona fide LBVs. Modern time-domain surveys provide homogeneous light curves for many Galactic massive stars, but each survey has its own limitations in terms of depth, temporal coverage, and observing cadence. Using confirmed Galactic LBVs as a control sample, we aim to test what Gaia DR3 and complementary photometric surveys can and cannot establish about LBV-type variability. We assembled a vetted sample of 75 Galactic LBVs and cLBVs with near- and mid-infrared photometry from 2MASS, MSX, WISE, GLIMPSE, and MIPSGAL. The infrared material was used to validate identifications, evaluate source confusion, and place objects in a circumstellar-dust context. We then constructed light curves from Gaia DR3, the Bochum survey, the ASAS SN, and the ZTF, and analyzed large-amplitude and periodic cases with Lomb-Scargle (LS) and phase dispersion minimization (PDM) methods. Gaia DR3 matches are available for 67% of the sample and 76% are reported as variable. We identify high-amplitude variables and periodic systems that may be binaries rather than classical LBVs. Six confirmed LBVs and five candidates show variations larger than 0.6 mag in the Gaia RP filter. Their light curves are examined and three periodic variables are identified. The light curves of OMN2000 LS1 and DWC2011 140 show primary and secondary minima, strongly suggesting eclipsing binary systems. OMN2000 LS1 has a well-constrained period of 80.29 d, and DWC2011 140 of 95.07 d.

AI.tldr: Using 75 Galactic LBVs and candidate LBVs with multi-wavelength photometry, this study tests what Gaia DR3 and complementary surveys can establish about LBV variability, identifying high-amplitude and periodic (likely eclipsing binary) systems among them.
AI.motivation: Candidate LBVs (cLBVs) share LBV-like spectra and circumstellar nebulae but lack the long-term light curves needed to confirm bona fide LBV status. Modern time-domain surveys offer homogeneous photometry yet differ in depth, cadence, and coverage, so it is unclear how reliably they can establish LBV-type variability.
AI.method: The authors assemble a vetted sample of 75 Galactic LBVs and cLBVs with near- and mid-infrared photometry (2MASS, MSX, WISE, GLIMPSE, MIPSGAL) to validate identifications, assess source confusion, and characterize circumstellar dust. Using confirmed LBVs as a control sample, they build light curves from Gaia DR3, the Bochum survey, ASAS SN, and ZTF, and analyze large-amplitude and periodic cases with Lomb-Scargle and phase dispersion minimization (PDM) methods.
AI.result: Gaia DR3 matches exist for 67% of the sample, with 76% reported as variable. Six confirmed LBVs and five candidates show >0.6 mag variation in Gaia RP; three periodic variables are identified. OMN2000 LS1 and DWC2011 140 exhibit primary and secondary minima strongly suggesting eclipsing binaries, with well-constrained periods of 80.29 d and 95.07 d, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Gaia DR3 plus complementary surveys can recover and characterize LBV-type variability but also reveal contaminating high-amplitude and periodic (binary) variables. Some putative LBV variability is attributable to eclipsing binaries rather than classical S Doradus-type behavior, underscoring the need for long-term, multi-survey light curves in classifying cLBVs.

title: Constraining the Binary Fraction and Mass-Ratio Distribution of FGK Dwarfs with Gaia XP Spectra: Metallicity, $α$-Element, and Age Dependencies
comment: 24 pages, 17 figures plus 1 online figure set with 2 additional figures, 5 tables, accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: We present a study of the binary fraction and mass-ratio distribution for near 200,000 FGK dwarf stars within 1 kpc, utilizing the Stellar Locus Outlier (SLOT) method applied to synthetic Gaia XP photometry and stellar parameters from LAMOST DR9. By modeling the asymmetric color residuals relative to a metallicity-dependent single-star locus, we measure the binary fraction $f_b$ and constrain the power-law slope $γ_{\rm large\,q}$ of the mass-ratio distribution at high mass ratio $q$. Higher metallicity is associated with a steeper (more negative) $γ_{{\rm large}q}$, indicating a larger proportion of low-mass-ratio systems. For $α$-elements, [Mg/H] and [Si/H] are anticorrelated with $f_b$ in thin-disk-dominated subsamples; conversely, [Ca/H] shows a positive correlation with $f_b$ in thin-disk-dominated subsamples. No correlation is found between $f_b$ and $α$-element abundances in thick-disk-dominated subsamples. The binary fraction increases modestly toward older ages in the thin-disk population, a trend that likely reflects underlying correlations with chemistry. Our results shed light on how chemical composition and dynamical processes shape the binary properties of solar-type stars.

AI.tldr: Using SLOT applied to synthetic Gaia XP photometry plus LAMOST DR9 parameters for ~200,000 FGK dwarfs within 1 kpc, we measure the binary fraction and high-mass-ratio slope of the mass-ratio distribution and link them to metallicity, α-elements, and age.
AI.motivation: Binary properties of solar-type stars are shaped by both chemical composition and dynamical processes, but large, homogeneous samples with well-characterized chemistry are needed to disentangle these effects across the thin and thick disk.
AI.method: The Stellar Locus Outlier (SLOT) method is applied to synthetic Gaia XP photometry combined with LAMOST DR9 stellar parameters for ~200,000 FGK dwarfs within 1 kpc; asymmetric color residuals relative to a metallicity-dependent single-star locus are modeled to infer the binary fraction f_b and the power-law slope γ_large q of the mass-ratio distribution at high q.
AI.result: Higher metallicity correlates with a steeper (more negative) γ_large q, i.e., more low-mass-ratio systems. In thin-disk-dominated subsamples, [Mg/H] and [Si/H] anticorrelate with f_b while [Ca/H] correlates positively; no f_b–α-element correlation appears in thick-disk-dominated subsamples. Binary fraction increases modestly with age in the thin disk.
AI.conclusion: Chemical composition and dynamical processes jointly shape the binary properties of solar-type stars; the age trend in the thin disk likely reflects underlying chemical correlations rather than an independent age effect.

title: The W Transform: an additional powerful tool for astrophysical time-series analysis
comment: 25 pages, 11 figures, accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: This work introduces the W Transform (WT) for astrophysical applications and explores its similarities and differences to the Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT), in photometric stellar light curves (LCs). We tested both techniques on synthetic data, producing LCs with different noise levels and numbers of gaps, and applied them to LCs from TESS space mission. The analysis focused on six stars: the solar analog TIC 276293046, the ultra-cool dwarf TIC 359892714, the $γ$ Dor pulsator TIC 164173105, the eclipsing binary TIC 355151781, the hosting planet star TIC 142276270, and the brown dwarf TIC 102076870. Overall, the results were in agreement, except for stars with LCs presenting sector-to-sector differences in structures or changes in the number of gaps, reflecting time-dynamic effects in the same target, which affect how time-dependent variability features appear in the time-frequency representation. For such LCs, the WT spectra are more stable and accurate in recovering signal amplitudes than the CWT maps, which exhibit distortions and limitations, showing that the inherent flexibility of the WT method in adjusting the dominant frequency could enhance time resolution even in LCs with complex or variable structures. We conclude that the WT is a robust tool for the analysis of stellar LCs, and that both methods may complement each other in an in-depth analysis of a periodic astrophysical signal. The present results suggest that the WT is a robust and accurate tool for analyzing stellar LCs, expanding the range of numerical techniques available for analyzing different stellar periodic phenomena from photometric observations.

AI.tldr: The W Transform (WT) is introduced for stellar photometric light curve analysis and benchmarked against the Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT), showing comparable performance overall but greater stability and amplitude-recovery accuracy for light curves with sector-to-sector structural changes or varying gaps.
AI.motivation: Stellar light curves from photometric surveys exhibit time-dependent variability, gaps, and noise that challenge time-frequency analysis. The authors aim to evaluate whether the WT offers advantages over the established CWT for such data and to characterize where the two methods diverge.
AI.method: Both WT and CWT were applied to synthetic light curves with controlled noise levels and gap counts, and to TESS light curves of six targets spanning distinct variability classes: a solar analog (TIC 276293046), an ultra-cool dwarf (TIC 359892714), a γ Dor pulsator (TIC 164173105), an eclipsing binary (TIC 355151781), a planet-hosting star (TIC 142276270), and a brown dwarf (TIC 102076870). Comparisons focused on time-frequency representation, signal amplitude recovery, and spectral stability.
AI.result: WT and CWT results were generally in agreement. Divergence appeared for stars whose light curves show sector-to-sector structural differences or changes in gap number, i.e., time-dynamic effects. In these cases, WT spectra were more stable and recovered signal amplitudes more accurately, whereas CWT maps showed distortions and limitations. The WT's flexibility in adjusting the dominant frequency improved time resolution even for complex or variable structures.
AI.conclusion: The WT is a robust and accurate tool for analyzing stellar light curves, extending the numerical toolkit for studying periodic stellar phenomena from photometric observations. WT and CWT are best regarded as complementary, with combined use supporting in-depth analysis of periodic astrophysical signals.

title: The Alma catalog of OB stars. IV. A massive star census of the Magellanic Clouds System
comment: The catalog is available for download via CDS
summary:
Context. The Magellanic Clouds System (MCS), comprising the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds (LMC and SMC) and the Magellanic Bridge (MB), offers a nearby laboratory for studying massive stars. Existing catalogs are limited by extinction, crowding, and incomplete cross-validation with the literature.
  Aims. We identify candidate stars with initial masses of roughly 8 solar masses or more, including O- and early-B-type stars, supergiants, luminous blue variables, and Wolf-Rayet stars. We aim to improve completeness in reddened and crowded regions and recover sources missed by large surveys.
  Methods. We combine Gaia DR3 astrometry and photometry with SIMBAD, HST, and complementary optical and infrared surveys. We select candidates using color-magnitude and color-color diagrams, extinction tracks, Gaia astrometry and variability, and spectral classifications. We check for duplicates and multiple systems, include literature and HST-resolved sources without reliable Gaia counterparts, especially in 30 Dor, and derive synthetic Gaia photometry where Gaia measurements are incomplete.
  Results. ALS IV contains 51 954 massive star candidates: 36 506 in the LMC, 15 264 in the SMC, and 184 in the MB. It provides homogeneous identifiers and coordinates, multiwavelength photometry, astrometry, variability diagnostics, and spectral classifications where available. Complementary photometry and HST observations recover reddened and crowded sources missed by Gaia-based selections. The sample traces the main massive-star populations and prominent star-forming regions across the MCS.
  Conclusions. ALS IV provides the most comprehensive census of massive star candidates in the MCS and serves as a reference for massive-star studies and future surveys and Gaia releases.

AI.tldr: ALS IV is a new catalog of 51,954 massive star candidates across the Magellanic Clouds System, built by combining Gaia DR3 with multiwavelength data to overcome extinction, crowding, and survey incompleteness.
AI.motivation: Existing massive-star catalogs in the Magellanic Clouds System (LMC, SMC, and Magellanic Bridge) are limited by extinction, crowding, and incomplete cross-validation with the literature, leaving reddened and crowded regions and survey-missed sources poorly characterized.
AI.method: The authors combine Gaia DR3 astrometry and photometry with SIMBAD, HST, and complementary optical/infrared surveys. Candidates (initial mass ≳8 solar masses: O- and early-B stars, supergiants, LBVs, Wolf-Rayet stars) are selected via color-magnitude and color-color diagrams, extinction tracks, Gaia astrometry and variability, and spectral classifications. They remove duplicates, account for multiple systems, include literature and HST-resolved sources lacking reliable Gaia counterparts (notably in 30 Dor), and derive synthetic Gaia photometry where measurements are incomplete.
AI.result: ALS IV contains 51,954 massive star candidates: 36,506 in the LMC, 15,264 in the SMC, and 184 in the Magellanic Bridge. It provides homogeneous identifiers, coordinates, multiwavelength photometry, astrometry, variability diagnostics, and available spectral classifications. Complementary photometry and HST data recover reddened and crowded sources missed by Gaia-based selection, and the sample traces the main massive-star populations and prominent star-forming regions across the system.
AI.conclusion: ALS IV offers the most comprehensive census of massive star candidates in the Magellanic Clouds System to date and serves as a reference catalog for massive-star studies as well as for planning future surveys and Gaia data releases.

title: MINDS: The mid-infrared spectrum of the disk, jets, and winds of DG Tau
comment: 30 pages, 28 figures, 2 tables. Accepted (22 October 2026) for publication in Astronomy and Astrophysics
summary: DG Tau is one of the best-studied young stellar objects in transition from a Class I protostar to a T Tauri star. It is no longer embedded in a dense molecular cloud, but still reveals features that are commonly seen in protostars at earlier evolutionary stages. DG Tau hosts a protoplanetary disk and two energetic jets that can be studied down to the immediate environment of the star and disk at optical, infrared, and X-ray wavelengths. We use the Medium Resolution Spectrometer of MIRI on the James Webb Space Telescope. DG Tau's mid-infrared spectrum consists of a very bright continuum with various silicate features, and lines of CO, H$_2$O, OH, H I, H$_2$, Ne$^{+}$, Ne$^{2+}$, Ar$^{+}$, Fe$^{+}$, and Ni$^{+}$. We find substantial grain growth to at least 2 $μ$m at an early evolutionary stage. Lines of H$_2$O and CO are formed at extremely high temperatures (600-2000 K). The ratio of warm to hot water is the lowest among previous observations of disks with JWST. This and a very strong continuum point toward the relevance of the strong accretion of DG Tau and consequently strong stellar UV irradiation. The pair of jets reveals a rich spectrum of emission lines from ions, in particular producing forbidden lines of [Ne II], [Ne III], [Ar II], [Fe II], and [Ni II]. The forward jet shows a collimated structure as found previously, while the hitherto poorly described, receding jet is more widely dispersed on scales of several arcsec, showing a layered structure with the fastest components being the most collimated. The ionization of the jet gas cannot be reconciled with high-energy radiation from the star itself. Instead, we propose a unified nonequilibrium ionization shock model in which the previously studied X-ray jet plasma continuously cools, recombining ions until, at temperatures around $10^4$ K and below, metals at low ionization stages emit the observed ion lines.

AI.tldr: JWST/MIRI medium-resolution spectroscopy of the Class I-to-T Tauri transition object DG Tau reveals strong grain growth to 2 μm, hot (600–2000 K) water and CO from accretion-driven UV heating, and jet emission best explained by a cooling, recombining nonequilibrium shock model.
AI.motivation: DG Tau is a benchmark young stellar object caught between Class I and T Tauri stages, still showing protostellar features despite no longer being embedded. Its disk and two jets can be probed down to the star-disk environment, making it an ideal laboratory to test grain evolution, inner-disk heating, and jet ionization at an early evolutionary phase—questions previously limited by spectral coverage and sensitivity.
AI.method: Medium Resolution Spectrometer (MRS) observations with MIRI on JWST, yielding mid-infrared spectra of the disk and both the forward and receding jets. Spectral analysis covers the bright continuum, silicate features, and atomic/molecular lines (CO, H2O, OH, H I, H2, Ne+, Ne2+, Ar+, Fe+, Ni+), including spatially resolved characterization of jet structure and ionization.
AI.result: Substantial grain growth to at least 2 μm at an early evolutionary stage; H2O and CO emitting at 600–2000 K; the lowest warm-to-hot water ratio yet seen in JWST disk observations, together with a very strong continuum, indicating intense accretion and strong stellar UV irradiation. Both jets show rich forbidden-line emission ([Ne II], [Ne III], [Ar II], [Fe II], [Ni II]); the forward jet is collimated, while the receding jet is widely dispersed over several arcsec with a layered structure in which the fastest components are the most collimated. Jet ionization cannot be explained by stellar high-energy radiation.
AI.conclusion: A unified nonequilibrium ionization shock model is proposed: pre-existing X-ray jet plasma cools and recombines, and at ~10^4 K and below, low-ionization-stage metals emit the observed forbidden lines. DG Tau thus links accretion-driven inner-disk heating, rapid grain growth, and shock-ionized jets within a single early-stage system.

title: TESS discovers an eclipse of the Be star V1294 Aql (= HD 184279) by its not-so-small, low-mass companion
comment: 6 pgs, 4 figures. Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics Letters
summary: In a single sector of observations with the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS), an eclipse-like event occurred in the Be star V1294 Aql. The reality of the eclipse is corroborated by $UBV$ photometry from the Hvar observatory. The event occurred at phase 17.97 of the linear ephemeris by Harmanec et al. (2022) for the upper conjunction of this SB1 binary (P$_{\rm orb}$ = 192.9 d). Therefore, we conclude that the Be star was eclipsed by its companion. With this elimination of the uncertainty of the orbital inclination, the mass of the secondary is 0.99 to 1.17 M$_\odot$ for masses of the primary from 14 to 18 M$_{\odot}$. The depth of the eclipse of $\sim$6.0% (0.06 mag) is incompatible with a white-dwarf (WD) nature of the companion. At the implied radius of $\sim$25% of that of the B0.5 primary, the secondary is not a bona-fide sdO/sdB star, either, but it could be still in its contraction phase. The increasing number of such stars may lend support to model calculations according to which the timescale of the contraction can be not thermal but instead is governed by the much slower removal of a residual H-rich envelope. It is also possible the companion is on the pre-main sequence in which case the two stars have not yet interacted. Two new interferometric observations were obtained near orbital quadrature but the secondary star was not detected, nor was it detected in high-resolution high-S/N echelle spectra.

AI.tldr: A TESS eclipse of the Be star V1294 Aql confirms that the system is eclipsing, breaking the inclination degeneracy and constraining the nature of the unseen companion to a subgiant-like object rather than a white dwarf.
AI.motivation: The companion in the SB1 binary V1294 Aql was previously unconstrained in mass because the orbital inclination was unknown, leaving open whether it is a white dwarf, an sdO/sdB star, or a pre-main-sequence object.
AI.method: A single-sector TESS light curve revealed an eclipse-like event, corroborated by UBV photometry from Hvar at phase 17.97 of the Harmanec et al. (2022) ephemeris; the eclipse depth, implied secondary radius, and mass range were derived, supplemented by two new interferometric observations near quadrature and high-resolution, high-S/N echelle spectroscopy.
AI.result: The eclipse depth of ~6.0% (0.06 mag) implies a secondary radius of ~25% of the B0.5 primary and a mass of 0.99–1.17 M_sun for primary masses of 14–18 M_sun; the companion was not detected interferometrically or spectroscopically.
AI.conclusion: The companion is not a white dwarf and not a bona fide sdO/sdB star; it may be a contracting object with a residual H-rich envelope (slow, non-thermal contraction) or a pre-main-sequence star in a system that has not yet interacted.

title: Multi-Frequency Inversion of Meridional Flows Using Wave-Simulation-Based Sensitivity Kernels: Kernels, Method and Validation On Synthetic Data
summary:
Measuring the solar meridional circulation is central to understanding how magnetic flux and angular momentum are redistributed within the Sun. While time-distance helioseismology has been a primary tool for probing these internal flows, current methods generally rely on broadband travel-time measurements that compress the frequency dependence of the wavefield into single values for each measurement geometry. This approach overlooks the fact that different temporal frequencies sample the solar interior differently, potentially limiting our ability to resolve complex, depth-dependent flow structures. In this paper, we present a framework for performing meridional circulation inversions using frequency-dependent travel-time shifts and corresponding sensitivity kernels derived directly from global-scale, 3D wave-propagation simulations.
  We analyze sensitivities for horizontal and radial flows, noting that higher temporal frequencies offer increased spatial resolution while their practical application is balanced by the lower signal--to--noise ratio of travel-time measurements at frequencies above the 3 mHz peak of solar oscillations. Using an iterative regularized least-squares solver, we demonstrate that our method successfully recovers many aspects of complex circulation models while remaining robust against the stochastic noise of realistic simulations. We consider the impact of different regularization operators on the inversions, and enforcing constraints like mass conservation to improve inversion results.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a frequency-dependent time-distance helioseismology framework for solar meridional circulation inversion, using travel-time shifts and sensitivity kernels from global 3D wave-propagation simulations.
AI.motivation: Current meridional circulation inversions rely on broadband travel-time measurements that collapse the frequency dependence of the wavefield into single values per geometry, overlooking that different temporal frequencies sample the interior differently and potentially limiting resolution of depth-dependent flows.
AI.method: Frequency-dependent travel-time shifts with corresponding sensitivity kernels derived directly from global-scale 3D wave-propagation simulations; analysis of sensitivities for horizontal and radial flows; iterative regularized least-squares inversion tested on complex circulation models with stochastic noise, comparing regularization operators and enforcing constraints such as mass conservation.
AI.result: Higher temporal frequencies yield improved spatial resolution but are limited by lower signal-to-noise ratio above the ~3 mHz oscillation peak; the inversion recovers many aspects of complex circulation models while remaining robust to realistic stochastic noise, and constraints like mass conservation improve results.
AI.conclusion: Frequency-dependent travel-time inversion provides a viable path to better resolve depth-dependent meridional circulation, with performance governed by a resolution–signal-to-noise tradeoff and improved by appropriate regularization and physical constraints.

title: A Study of Three Intrinsically Luminous Long Period Interacting Eclipsing Binaries in the Galaxy and the Small Magellanic Cloud
summary: The properties of the eclipsing binaries SMC004701.39-732645.8, SMC005609.41-722809.2 and PW Pup are examined using archival photometric and spectroscopic observations. These systems have orbital periods of hundreds of days, and contain highly evolved components with temperature differences of at least 1000 - 2000K. The SMC systems are among the brightest eclipsing binaries in that galaxy at visible wavelengths, and show excess thermal emission that appears to be typical for luminous K and M giants in that galaxy. A preliminary mass function for SMC004701 suggests a minimum mass for the secondary of 3.8 +/- 0.8 Msolar, whereas the PW Pup mass function indicates a minimum mass for the secondary of 3.2 +/- 0.3 Msolar. Light curve elements are examined for a range of mass ratios using observations at visible and mid-infrared (MIR) wavelengths. The results suggest that SMC004701 may prove to be a double line spectroscopic binary at visible wavelengths. However, with the possible exception of emission from a circumstellar disk, infrared observations will likely be required to detect light from the secondary in the other two systems. All three systems have likely experienced mass transfer, and had components with initial masses that correspond to B spectral types on the main sequence. The light associated with the secondary likely originates from a shell or disk that obscures a hotter central star.

AI.tldr: Analysis of three long-period eclipsing binaries (SMC004701.39-732645.8, SMC005609.41-722809.2, PW Pup) using archival photometric and spectroscopic data, characterizing their evolved components, mass functions, and evidence of mass transfer.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to characterize luminous, long-period eclipsing binaries with highly evolved components, particularly the brightest such systems in the SMC, to constrain their masses, mass ratios, and evolutionary history.
AI.method: Archival photometric and spectroscopic observations are used to derive orbital periods, temperature differences, and preliminary mass functions. Light curve elements are modeled over a range of mass ratios using visible and mid-infrared (MIR) data.
AI.result: The systems have orbital periods of hundreds of days and components differing in temperature by at least 1000-2000 K. SMC004701 yields a minimum secondary mass of 3.8 +/- 0.8 Msolar; PW Pup yields 3.2 +/- 0.3 Msolar. The SMC systems show excess thermal emission typical of luminous K and M giants in that galaxy.
AI.conclusion: SMC004701 may be a double-line spectroscopic binary at visible wavelengths, while the secondaries in the other two systems likely require infrared observations (absent circumstellar disk emission) to detect. All three systems likely underwent mass transfer, with initial component masses corresponding to B spectral types on the main sequence; the secondary's light likely arises from a shell or disk obscuring a hotter central star.
